intro: A probability for a normal variable is an area under its curve; for a binomial count it is the total height of some bars. Drag the boundary, pick the direction, and read the probability. Each answer is written the way the exam wants it: the distribution, its parameters, the boundary and the direction.
howItWorks:
Every area is computed exactly: the normal one from the standard normal distribution after $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$, the binomial one by adding $P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k}p^k(1 - p)^{n - k}$ over every count in the event. The shaded region is the region added up.

  • Table or technology. Table A gives the area to the left of $z$ rounded to two places. Its answer can differ from technology in the third or fourth decimal; both are accepted.
  • Words to symbols. "At most 3" is $X \le 3$, "fewer than 3" is $X \le 2$, "at least 3" is $X \ge 3$, "more than 3" is $X \ge 4$. For a count the difference matters; for a normal variable it does not, because one value has probability 0.
  • The empirical rule. About 68%, 95% and 99.7% of a normal distribution lies within 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations of the mean. It is an approximation; the exact areas are 0.6827, 0.9545 and 0.9973.
  • The normal shape over a binomial. The curve with mean $np$ and SD $\sqrt{np(1 - p)}$ is drawn only to compare shapes. Every binomial probability here is exact.

Test yourself makes new problems from a seed (the problem code), checks every step against a key the validator recomputes independently, and names the usual slip when an answer misses.

contexts.setup: The heights of adult women in a large country are approximately normal with mean {mu} and standard deviation {sd}.
contexts.less: What is the probability that a randomly chosen woman is shorter than {b}?
contexts.more: What is the probability that a randomly chosen woman is taller than {a}?
contexts.between: What is the probability that a randomly chosen woman is between {a} and {b} tall?
contexts.low: What height marks the shortest {pct} of adult women?
contexts.high: How tall must a woman be to be among the tallest {pct}?

contexts.setup: One driver's commute times are approximately normal with mean {mu} and standard deviation {sd}.
contexts.less: What is the probability that a randomly chosen commute takes less than {b}?
contexts.more: What is the probability that a randomly chosen commute takes more than {a}?
contexts.between: What is the probability that a randomly chosen commute takes between {a} and {b}?
contexts.low: What commute time marks the fastest {pct} of this driver's commutes?
contexts.high: What commute time marks the slowest {pct} of this driver's commutes?

contexts.setup: A machine fills cereal boxes with weights that are approximately normal with mean {mu} and standard deviation {sd}.
contexts.less: What is the probability that a randomly chosen box holds less than {b}?
contexts.more: What is the probability that a randomly chosen box holds more than {a}?
contexts.between: What is the probability that a randomly chosen box holds between {a} and {b}?
contexts.low: What weight marks the lightest {pct} of boxes?
contexts.high: What weight marks the heaviest {pct} of boxes?

contexts.setup: Scores on a state reading test are approximately normal with mean {mu} and standard deviation {sd}.
contexts.less: What is the probability that a randomly chosen student scores below {b}?
contexts.more: What is the probability that a randomly chosen student scores above {a}?
contexts.between: What is the probability that a randomly chosen student scores between {a} and {b}?
contexts.low: What score marks the lowest {pct} of students?
contexts.high: What score must a student reach to be in the top {pct}?

contexts.setup: A basketball player makes each free throw with probability {p}, independently of other shots. She takes {n} free throws.
contexts.X: the number of free throws she makes

contexts.setup: A student guesses at random on {n} multiple-choice questions, each with probability {p} of a correct guess.
contexts.X: the number of questions the student gets right

contexts.setup: Each seed in a packet sprouts with probability {p}, independently of the others. A gardener plants {n} seeds.
contexts.X: the number of seeds that sprout

contexts.setup: In a large city, a proportion {p} of adults ride a bike to work at least once a week. A random sample of {n} adults is chosen.
contexts.X: the number of adults in the sample who ride a bike to work at least once a week
contexts.event: {k} of the adults in the sample ride a bike to work at least once a week
